subject: physics
title: Series and parallel circuits
key_idea: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere, the potential difference is shared and resistances add. In a parallel circuit each branch has the same potential difference, the currents add and the total resistance is smaller.

blocks.text: In a series circuit the components are joined one after another in a single loop. There is only one path for the current.

items: The **current** is the same through each component.
The total **potential difference** of the power supply is shared between the components.
The total **resistance** is the sum of the resistances of the components.

blocks.label: Total resistance in series
where: R₁, R₂ = resistance of each component, in ohms (Ω)

items.text: In series the supply potential difference is shared between the components.
A 3.0 V battery is connected in series to a 22 Ω resistor and a resistor X. The potential difference across X is 2.1 V.

items: An **ammeter** is connected in series with the component, so the same current passes through it.
A **voltmeter** is connected in parallel across the component.

diagram.alt: Change the supply and two resistors in series to see the total resistance, current and potential difference across the second resistor.
Find the current in a series circuit of two resistors.
diagram.question: Two resistors of {R1} Ω and {R2} Ω are connected in series to a {V} V battery. Calculate the current in the circuit.

items: Series: same current, shared potential difference, resistances add.
Adding another resistor in series increases the total resistance.
A switch in a series circuit must be closed for the current to flow.

blocks.text: In a parallel circuit the components are on separate branches. There is more than one path for the current. Some circuits have both series and parallel parts.

items: The **potential difference** across each component is the same.
The total **current** through the whole circuit is the sum of the currents through the separate components.
The total **resistance** of two resistors is less than the resistance of the smallest individual resistor.
Current is conserved at a junction. The current going in equals the current coming out.
For example, 6.0 A flows into a junction and 3.5 A flows out along one wire. The current in the other wire is 6.0 − 3.5 = 2.5 A.
Parallel: same potential difference across each branch, currents add.
The total resistance is less than the smallest resistor.
Current is conserved at a junction.

blocks.text: Adding resistors in series raises the total resistance. Adding resistors in parallel lowers it. The reasons are different.

rows: Splits between branches and adds up

items: In series the current must pass through every resistor, so each one adds to the resistance.
In parallel the extra branch gives the charge another path. More current flows for the same potential difference, so the total resistance falls.
More resistors in series: total resistance increases.
More resistors in parallel: total resistance decreases, because there are more paths for the current.

checks.q: Two resistors of 10 Ω and 15 Ω are in series. State their total resistance.
Explain why the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is less than the smallest resistance.
checks.a: There are more paths for the current. More current flows for the same potential difference, so the total resistance is lower.

checks.q: A 3.0 V battery is connected across two resistors in series. The potential difference across one is 2.1 V. State the potential difference across the other.

exam_phrases: the total resistance must be less than 20 Ω
the total resistance of the resistors (in parallel) is less than the resistance of the smallest resistor
more than one path for charge to flow
the current would be higher (for the same p.d.)
(both) switches need to be closed / on

mistakes.wrong: The total resistance of 20 Ω and R in parallel is 26 Ω.
mistakes.right: In parallel the total is less than the smallest resistance, so it must be less than 20 Ω.

mistakes.wrong: Connecting two resistors in parallel increases the total resistance.
mistakes.right: It decreases. Give a reason: more than one path for charge to flow, or the total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance. The reason scores only if the box is right.

mistakes.wrong: When the light intensity decreases, the current in the LDR increases.
mistakes.right: When the light intensity decreases, the potential difference across the LDR increases and the current decreases.

worked_example.question:
A student used resistors to model solid tissue and water in a person's legs. The student connected a 20 Ω resistor in parallel with a resistor, R.

The student calculated the total resistance of the two resistors. The student's answer was 26 Ω.

Explain why the student's answer cannot be correct.
answer_points: The total resistance must be less than 20 Ω.
Because the total resistance of resistors in parallel is less than the resistance of the smallest resistor.
worked_example.tip: One mark for the statement and one for the reason.

exam_phrases: effective resistance = sum of individual resistances

mistakes.wrong: The current in wire H is 6.0 + 3.5 = 9.5 A.
mistakes.right: Current is conserved at a junction. The current in H is 2.5 A, found by subtracting 3.5 A from 6.0 A, not by adding.

mistakes.wrong: The voltage across the 22 Ω resistor is 2.1 V.
mistakes.right: 2.1 V is across resistor X. The supply is shared, so across the 22 Ω resistor it is 3.0 − 2.1 = 0.9 V.

mistakes.wrong: Removing a resistor from a parallel circuit decreases the total resistance.
mistakes.right: Fewer resistors in parallel means the total resistance increases. The current decreases and the voltage stays the same.

worked_example.question:
Some students investigate resistors in parallel.

The students set up a circuit containing four identical resistors. They measure the current from the power supply and the voltage (p.d.) across the resistors. They remove one resistor and measure again, then repeat with 2 resistors and with 1 resistor.

number of resistors | current in mA | voltage in V
4 | (not recorded) | 6.00
3 | 27.3 | 6.00
2 | 18.2 | 6.00
1 | 9.1 | 6.00

Using data from the table, explain what happens to the total resistance of the circuit as the number of resistors in parallel decreases.
answer_points: And the voltage stays the same.
worked_example.tip: Link the three points: current falls while the voltage is constant, so the resistance rises. Fewer paths for the current is also credited.

mistakes.wrong: The maximum resistance from four resistors comes from connecting them in parallel.
mistakes.right: Resistors in series have a bigger total than any one of them. The maximum is when all four are in series: the resistances add.

mistakes.wrong: B and D have the same resistance, with no working shown.
mistakes.right: Name the pair and show the resistance of each using resistance = voltage ÷ current. Both parts are needed for the mark.

worked_example.question:
A student takes voltage and current measurements for four resistors.

Resistor A: 12.0 V, 2.0 A
Resistor B: 6.0 V, 1.5 A
Resistor C: 7.5 V, 1.5 A
Resistor D: 8.0 V, 2.0 A

Calculate the maximum resistance that can be made using all four resistors.
answer_points: Find each resistance from R = V ÷ I: A = 6 Ω, B = 4 Ω, C = 5 Ω, D = 4 Ω.
The maximum is with all four in series: 6 + 4 + 5 + 4 = 19 Ω.
worked_example.tip: Error carried forward is allowed from the earlier resistance values.
